paragraphs.source_en: Men who defended their women were being slaughtered.105 Meanwhile, churches, including Hagia Sophia, were stripped of valuables and sacred treasures. The priceless altar of the Great Church was hacked to bits to be divided among the victors. A French prostitute dressed up in the patriarch’s garb and put on a show. Much of the sacred loot was later shipped out to the west, where it remains today in museums, treasuries, and sacristies, espe- cially in Venice. It included icons, relics, ancient statues (such as the porphyry 724 A New Paradigm Tetrarchs and the so-​called Horses of St. Mark), and even entire architectural elements (the co-​called Pilastri Acritani, taken from the ruins of Anicia Juliana’s church of St. Polyeuktos). The abbot of a Cistercian abbey in Alsatia made a beeline for the Pantokrator monastery, knowing that other Latins were not as aware of its significance.

paragraphs.source_en: He threatened a monk there with death in order to seize the holy treasures that graced the tomb of Manuel Komnenos, ironically a Latinophile emperor. One of the pieces that he stole from there was a tablet that contained relics and depicted the Last Supper: he gave it to the German king Philipp of Swabia, one of the prime diverters of the crusade, explaining to him that the Greek emperors used to wear it around their neck on special occasions “as a token of their imperial power.” This was as close as Philipp got to wielding eastern power.106 A mosaic celebrating the capture of City was erected in a church in Ravenna, ironically a city that had once been Constantinople’s forward operating base in Italy.107 For centuries, wealth and people had flowed into Constantinople; now they began to flow out.

paragraphs.source_en: The Roman elite fled from the City rather than endure Latin rule, and many of the poor abandoned it as well. About a sixth of the City was a burned ruin, while the rest was stripped of valuables. Too late, the pope and others in the west realized that the project had been driven “more by price than by prayer.”108 As a result, “the beautiful City of Constantine, the common de- light and boast of all nations, was consumed and blackened by Causes of fire, captured by force, and hollowed out of its wealth by these decline in random western nations.”109 Constantinople would never the twelfth fully recover. Nor would the Romans.
